To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people who make a commitment to cooperate in a social dilemma are likely to honor that commitment, even if the decision is not made in a group context; and (2) people who make such a commitment are likely to honor it even if they are reminded that the decision is not final, and even if the decision to honor it is made after the decision to make the original commitment.

group discussion of social dilemma choices increases cooperation, that this increase is not moderated by whether the choices are made anonymously or publicly, that it is not moderated by the degree of mindfulness with which participants made their decisions, and that it is not due to mindless compliance with a prior choice.

group discussion of social dilemmas increases cooperation because people honor the commitments they made during the group discussion, but they do so because of the internal, not the social, consequences of doing so.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of personal norms in promoting cooperative behavior.
the question of whether people honor the commitments they have made in group discussion because of the social or the personal consequences of not doing so.
the conditions under which people honor commitments to cooperate as an internalized personal norm rather than as a social norm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of social dilemma discussion is not mediated by the social consequences of noncooperation.
group discussion of social dilemmas increases cooperation by increasing the internalization of norms to honor commitments.
group discussion of social dilemma increases cooperative behavior because of an internalized norm of commitment to cooperate, rather than because of social pressures to honor one's commitments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social consequences of breaking a commitment to cooperate in the group discussion are internalized by the individual, leading to an internalized personal norm to honor the commitment.
people do not honor their commitments because they are mindful of them or because they fear the social consequences of not honoring them.
people honor their commitments to cooperate because they have internalized a norm that they should keep their word.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are more likely to cooperate when they are part of a social group that has discussed the dilemma.
group discussion of social dilemmas can increase cooperation because people honor their prior commitments to cooperate.
the effect of group discussions on cooperative behavior is due to an internalized commitment norm rather than a mindless adherence to one's prior decision.
